description: Music, and down through music theory: scales, tuning, harmony, rhythm, and how the ear turns physics into feeling. Sound and waves themselves live under Machines.

concepts.title: Music
concepts.summary: Sound organized in time. Rhythm and pitch seem to move people almost everywhere, though what counts as harmony, or even as music, changes with the culture doing the listening.

concepts.title: Music Theory
concepts.summary: The vocabulary musicians use to describe what they do: notes, scales, chords, rhythms, and how they pull against each other. It's description after the fact, an attempt to name patterns that people already found by ear.

concepts.title: Scales
concepts.summary: A chosen ladder of pitches to build music from. Most cultures settle on five to seven notes per octave, and which ones they choose gives a tradition its recognizable color.

concepts.title: Modes
concepts.summary: The same seven notes, started from different places, give different moods: bright, dark, haunted, open. Each mode is a different set of intervals around a home note.

concepts.title: Pentatonic
concepts.summary: Five notes that sound good in almost any combination. Found in folk music from China to West Africa to the Scottish Highlands, it's what your fingers fall on when you improvise.

concepts.title: Tuning
concepts.summary: Deciding exactly which pitches count. It looks simple until you find that pure ratios can't close a circle, and every tuning system is a compromise between purity and playing in every key.

concepts.title: Harmonic Series
concepts.summary: Pluck a string and it vibrates as a whole and in halves, thirds, quarters at once. Those overtones are where the octave, fifth, and major third come from, and why some notes just sound related.

concepts.title: Equal Temperament
concepts.summary: Divide the octave into twelve identical steps. Every interval is slightly off from the pure ratio, but you can play in any key, which is why a modern piano can go anywhere.

concepts.title: Consonance
concepts.summary: Why some pairs of notes sound settled and others sound tense. Simple frequency ratios line up their overtones, and the ear likes that, though what counts as tense also depends on habit and culture.

concepts.title: Notation
concepts.summary: Writing sound down: pitch upward, time to the right. It let composers send a piece across centuries, and it shaped the music itself, favoring what could be written.

concepts.title: Harmony
concepts.summary: Notes sounding together. What music does with them, building tension and letting it resolve, is a large part of how it moves us.

concepts.title: Chords
concepts.summary: Three or more notes sounded at once. A handful of chord shapes and the ways they follow one another account for a vast amount of the music you know.

concepts.title: Tonality
concepts.summary: The sense that one note is home and the others lean toward it. Music sets up an expectation and then delays, fulfills, or tricks it, and that play of expectation is where much of the feeling comes from.

concepts.title: Counterpoint
concepts.summary: Two or more independent melodies woven together so each stands alone and they fit as well. Bach made it look effortless, and it's one of the deepest ideas in Western music.

concepts.title: Rhythm
concepts.summary: Pattern in time: strong beats and weak ones, long and short. It's the most physical part of music, and people synchronize to it, moving together, almost automatically.

concepts.title: Meter
concepts.summary: The grouping of beats into a repeating frame, such as twos, threes, or fours. It gives a piece its underlying walk or waltz, and lets the ear feel when something is deliberately off.

concepts.title: Tempo
concepts.summary: How fast the beat goes. Around the speed of a resting heart is where much of the world's music lives, which may not be a coincidence.

concepts.title: Melody
concepts.summary: A sequence of notes that the mind hears as a single shape. Melodies survive transposition and changes of instrument, which says the ear tracks the relationships and not the exact pitches.

concepts.title: Instruments
concepts.summary: Devices for making sound on purpose: strings, air columns, skins, keys. Each is a physical solution to controlling vibration, and its limits shape what music gets written for it.

concepts.title: The Piano
concepts.summary: A machine of strings and hammers that made the whole range of Western harmony available under ten fingers. It's part instrument, part mechanism, and part standard for how music is written down.

concepts.title: The Voice
concepts.summary: The first instrument. Air passes over vocal folds and the throat and mouth shape it, and no instrument has ever quite matched how directly it carries feeling.

concepts.title: Singing
concepts.summary: Speech stretched into pitch and held. People sing together in nearly every culture, and doing it in a group seems to line up breathing, heartbeat, and mood.

concepts.title: Silence
concepts.summary: The gaps that give sound its shape. Music is made as much of rests as notes, and a well-placed pause can say more than anything around it.
John Cage's piece in which the performer plays nothing for four minutes and thirty-three seconds. The point is the room: coughs, rain, breathing, everything you'd usually tune out becomes the music.

concepts.title: Improvisation
concepts.summary: Composing in real time, inside a set of rules. It's a conversation as much as a performance, and it depends on knowing the language well enough to stop thinking about it.

concepts.title: Jazz
concepts.summary: Music that grew from African American communities in the early twentieth century, built on rhythm, blues feeling, and improvisation. It turned the mistake into a tool and made listening a central skill.
